citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The EATE estimand: its reduction to ATE under no interference (Definitions 1 to 3 and the paragraph after Definition 3), the two displayed forms of EATE and ADSE, and Lemma A8
canonical_claim.location: Definitions 1 to 3 and the paragraph after Definition 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5). Definition 4 and the two displayed forms: p. 678 (PDF p. 6). Lemma A8: Supplement A, p. 7
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. The expected average treatment effect is a generalization of ATE in the sense that the two estimands coincide whenever the no-interference assumption holds. Under no interference, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$ does not depend on $\mathbf{z}$, so the marginalization is inconsequential. [p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] The difference becomes clear when the estimands are written in similar forms: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[y_i(1; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})] - \mathrm{E}[y_i(0; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})]\right)$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[y_i(1; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[y_i(0; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Supplement A, p. 7] LEMMA A8. Under Bernoulli randomization, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$. [The statements, with their hypotheses] (a) For any design: if the no-interference assumption holds, then $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ for every $\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^n$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$. (b) For any design, the displayed form of $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ holds; for any design with $0 < \Pr(Z_i = 1) < 1$ for all $i$, the displayed form of $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ holds. (c) Lemma A8.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H1; it held up for both readers and no finding touches it. All three parts are exact finite-population statements over the randomization distribution. The proof of Lemma A8 (Supplement A, p. 7) uses only that $Z_i$ and $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ are independent under a Bernoulli design. The claim that EATE is 'well defined under arbitrary interference' is carried by Definitions 2 and 3, which need no restriction on the potential outcomes.

canonical_claim.location: p. 681 (PDF p. 9); proof in Supplement A, Section 3, p. 5
canonical_claim.statement: LEMMA 1. $\max(C_1, n^{-1}C_\infty^2) \le d_{\mathrm{AVG}} \le C_2^2 \le C_\infty^2$. [No hypothesis is attached: the statement is for any interference indicators $I_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$ with $I_{ii} = 1$ arising from potential outcomes as on p. 680, with $d_{ij}$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_\infty$ as defined on p. 681.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [From the proof: Supplement A, p. 5] Note that $I_{ij} \le d_{ij} \le \sum_{\ell=1}^{n} I_{\ell i}I_{\ell j}$ by construction of Definition 5. $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n} I_{\ell i}I_{\ell j} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n} c_\ell^2 = C_2^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Part of headline claim P009-H3 (the lemma gives $C_1 \le d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, used for Corollary 1); it held up for both readers, one of whom also checked it on 2,000 random interference structures. Exact and purely combinatorial. For $n^{-1}C_\infty^2 \le d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$ the supplement argues through the configuration with the smallest $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$ for a given $C_\infty$; a direct argument is that if $c_\ell = C_\infty$ then $d_{ij} = 1$ for all $i, j$ with $I_{\ell i} = I_{\ell j} = 1$, which gives $n d_{\mathrm{AVG}} \ge C_\infty^2$. The companion bound $e_{\mathrm{AVG}} \le C_2^2$ (Lemma A7) is in the corrected-statement target for P009-E013.

canonical_claim.location: p. 695 (PDF p. 23); proof in Supplement A, Section 14, pp. 38–39
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 12. Given Assumption 7, $|\tau_{P\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} - \tau_{Q\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}}| \le 2k_\tau\delta(P, Q)$. [Hypotheses: $P$ and $Q$ are any two designs (probability measures on $\{0, 1\}^n$) for the same potential outcomes; Assumption 7 with constant $k_\tau$.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Designs and estimands under two designs: Section 7, p. 694 (PDF p. 22)] Let $P$ denote the probability measure of the design that was implemented, and let $Q$ be the probability measure of the alternative design. A subscript indicates which measure various probability operators refer to. $\tau_{P\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}_P[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$ and $\tau_{Q\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}_Q[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$. [Assumption 7: p. 694 (PDF p. 22)] ASSUMPTION 7 (Bounded unit-level effects). There exists a constant $k_\tau$ such that $|\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})| \le k_\tau$ for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^n$. [Total variation distance: pp. 694–695 (PDF pp. 22–23)] $\delta(P, Q) = \sup_{x \in \mathcal{F}}|P(x) - Q(x)|$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the event space of the designs, typically the power set of $\{0, 1\}^n$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H9; it held up for both readers and no finding touches it. Exact for every $n$. The proof (Supplement A, pp. 38–39) uses $|\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})| \le k_\tau$, $\sum_{\mathbf{z}}|P(\mathbf{z}) - Q(\mathbf{z})| = 2[P(A) - Q(A)]$ for $A = \{\mathbf{z} : P(\mathbf{z}) \ge Q(\mathbf{z})\}$, and $P(A) - Q(A) \le \delta(P, Q)$.

canonical_claim.location: p. 695 (PDF p. 23); proof in Supplement A, Section 14, pp. 39–41
canonical_claim.statement: LEMMA 2. Given Assumption 7, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$ is $2k_\tau n^{-1/r}C_{r/(r-1)}$-Lipschitz continuous with respect to the $L_r$ distance over $\{0, 1\}^n$ for any $r \ge 1$. [As restated at the start of its proof, Supplement A, p. 39] The lemma states that: $\left|\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}') - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}'')\right| \le 2k_\tau n^{-1/r}C_{r/(r-1)}\|\mathbf{z}' - \mathbf{z}''\|_r$ for any $\mathbf{z}', \mathbf{z}'' \in \{0, 1\}^n$ and $r \ge 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Designs and estimands under two designs: Section 7, p. 694 (PDF p. 22)] Let $P$ denote the probability measure of the design that was implemented, and let $Q$ be the probability measure of the alternative design. A subscript indicates which measure various probability operators refer to. $\tau_{P\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}_P[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$ and $\tau_{Q\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}_Q[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$. [Assumption 7: p. 694 (PDF p. 22)] ASSUMPTION 7 (Bounded unit-level effects). There exists a constant $k_\tau$ such that $|\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})| \le k_\tau$ for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^n$. [$L_r$ distance, as used in the proof of Lemma 2: Supplement A, pp. 39–41] $\|\mathbf{z}' - \mathbf{z}''\|_r = \left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}|z_i' - z_i''|^r\right]^{1/r}$ for $\mathbf{z}', \mathbf{z}'' \in \{0, 1\}^n$. $C_{r/(r-1)}$ is $C_p$ of p. 681 with $p = r/(r-1)$: $\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^{r/(r-1)}\right]^{\frac{r-1}{r}}$ (Supplement A, p. 41), and for $r = 1$ it is taken to be $C_\infty$ (p. 696).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H9; it held up for both readers. Exact for every $n$. The proof changes one coordinate at a time and reaches $\left|\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}') - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}'')\right| \le \frac{2k_\tau}{n}\sum_{v=1}^{n}|z_v' - z_v''|c_v$ (Supplement A, p. 40), then applies Hölder's inequality with conjugates $r$ and $r/(r - 1)$ (p. 41). For $r = 1$ the constant is $2k_\tau n^{-1}C_\infty$.

canonical_claim.location: p. 696 (PDF p. 24); proof in Supplement A, Section 14, p. 41
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 13. Given Assumption 7, $|\tau_{P\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} - \tau_{Q\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}}| \le 2k_\tau n^{-1/r}C_{r/(r-1)}W_r(P, Q)$. [Hypotheses: $P$ and $Q$ are any two designs on $\{0, 1\}^n$ for the same potential outcomes; Assumption 7 with constant $k_\tau$; $r \ge 1$ as in Lemma 2.]

A subscript indicates which measure various probability operators refer to. $\tau_{P\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}_P[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$ and $\tau_{Q\text{-}\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}_Q[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$. There exists a constant $k_\tau$ such that $|\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})| \le k_\tau$ for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^n$. [$L_r$ distance, as used in the proof of Lemma 2: Supplement A, pp. 39–41] $\|\mathbf{z}' - \mathbf{z}''\|_r = \left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}|z_i' - z_i''|^r\right]^{1/r}$ for $\mathbf{z}', \mathbf{z}'' \in \{0, 1\}^n$. $C_{r/(r-1)}$ is $C_p$ of p. 681 with $p = r/(r-1)$: $\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^{r/(r-1)}\right]^{\frac{r-1}{r}}$ (Supplement A, p. 41), and for $r = 1$ it is taken to be $C_\infty$ (p. 696). [Wasserstein metric: p. 696 (PDF p. 24)] Let $\mathcal{J}(P, Q)$ collect all distributions $(\mathbf{Z}', \mathbf{Z}'')$ over $\{0, 1\}^n \times \{0, 1\}^n$ such that the marginal distributions of $\mathbf{Z}'$ and $\mathbf{Z}''$ are $P$ and $Q$, respectively. $W_r(P, Q) = \inf_{J \in \mathcal{J}(P, Q)}\mathrm{E}_J\left[\|\mathbf{Z}' - \mathbf{Z}''\|_r\right]$, where the subscript denotes the underlying $L_r$ distance rather than the order of the Wasserstein metric, which is taken to be one here.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H9; it held up for both readers. Exact for every $n$. The paper derives it from Lemma 2 and the Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality theorem (Supplement A, p. 41). Only the elementary direction is needed: for every coupling $J \in \mathcal{J}(P, Q)$, $|\mathrm{E}_P[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})] - \mathrm{E}_Q[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]| = |\mathrm{E}_J[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z}') - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z}'')]| \le 2k_\tau n^{-1/r}C_{r/(r-1)}\mathrm{E}_J[\|\mathbf{Z}' - \mathbf{Z}''\|_r]$, and the infimum over $J$ gives the bound. On a finite space the infimum is attained.
